item.content:encoded: ML admins will be happy to learn that one bad GPU may no longer mean starting an entire training job from scratch. The latest 2.15 release of PyTorch includes a rewritten backend for Nvidia's Collective Communications Library (NCCL), designed to improve fault diagnosis and recovery when GPUs work together. This latest feature shows how its creators continue to advance the software from being a tool for researchers to being a cornerstone in production AI work. The interface to the networking library in PyTorch needed a rewrite – it was drowning in technical debt, said PyTorch core developer Tristan Rice , a Meta software engineer specializing in distributed computing, during a live YouTube livestream on Thursday. NCCL is pronounced "Nickel" and stands for the Nvidia Collective Communications Library. It provides PyTorch with a set of inter-GPU communication primitives, allowing GPUs to communicate within a single-node or across multi-node clusters, which is vital for running inference on large neural networks and for other tasks in building and maintaining LLMs. The old NCCL interface was too chaotic The previous PyTorch backend for NCCL, called ProcessGroupNCCL , could spawn dozens of communicators per process group, leading to intermittent deadlocks and unpredictable performance. The new version of the NCCL backend comes with a strict rule: One process group gets only one communicator during initialization. By default, this rule eliminates crosstalk between multiple communicators and all the complexities that entails. If a program requires parallelism, it will have to dispatch more process groups. The updated library also better handles stragglers by allowing for easier reconfiguration. If a GPU crashes or runs slowly, a third-party orchestrator can exclude the laggard and even assign a replacement worker. A “flight recorder” has also been added to give admins a better idea of what went wrong. Previously, if a cluster of GPUs stalled—perhaps from a timeout or deadlock—the user would just get a generic message. The new flight recorder captures all operations in a series of snapshots that can be inspected after a failure occurs. Rice noted the cleaned-up NCCL backend, also called ProcessGroupNCCL, will give developers a blank slate, making it easier to add new features. The legacy ProcessGroupNCCL is part of the 2.15 package as a rollback, but if the new NCCL backend works as expected, the older version will be removed in the 2.16 release, planned for early next year. Nvidia origins Why, you may ask, does a machine learning framework need a specialized communications library? Like NumPy, PyTorch supports numerical computing, but it also provides tools for building and training neural networks on CPUs and GPUs. In these environments, workers must constantly exchange data such as tensors, gradients, activations, and weights. The standard TCP-based networking stack can introduce bottlenecks in large GPU clusters, so NCCL uses optimized communication paths to move data between GPUs while reducing CPU overhead. Nvidia initially released NCCL at SC15 as a general-purpose accelerator, and it was adopted by the Facebook folks when they first built PyTorch in 2016. Their goal was to build a Python-based version of the Lua-based Torch ML library. “Every major ML lab (OpenAI, DeepMind, Meta, Nvidia) uses PyTorch. It powers everything from diffusion models and LLMs to recommender systems and robotics. This widespread adoption isn’t accidental,” noted Will Stewart, co-founder of AI software provider Northflank, in a blog post . More support for Apple and Nvidia’s next GPUs Other new features of PyTorch 2.15 include a new Python transport API for asynchronous one-way data movement – ideal for training jobs where weights are synchronized between trainers and generators – as well as parallel processing improvements for Apple gear and for supporting Nvidia’s next-generation Blackwell GPUs. Overall, the update consisted of 3,117 commits from 583 contributors. ®

item.title: US air traffic control enters the 21st century, starts to abandon floppy disks
item.description: The Federal Aviation Administration still uses computers that require floppy disks. But those are finally on the way out within the next few years. Yes, it’s still 2026, and yes, you read that right: The FAA – the agency responsible for overseeing aviation safety in the US – is finally getting rid of four systems dating back to the 1980s that remain in use at more than 400 facilities around the country, the agency announced on Thursday. “Good news America: floppy disks are out, 21st century tech is in,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in the FAA’s announcement. Only a few decades late, Sean, but we’re sure the flying public appreciates it. The new system, known as Enterprise Information Display System ( E-IDS ), is designed to consolidate data from various systems into a common digital platform, allowing air traffic controllers to access operational information and alerts needed to manage flights. E-IDS is replacing four legacy systems: Information Display System 4, used to track weather and operational info; the Automated Surface Observing System Controller Equipment Information Display System, which also relays weather information; the NAS Information Display System, which relays information about airports and other airspace conditions; and the En Route Information Display System (ERIDS), which handles information about flights. The FAA said E-IDS will improve how Pilot Reports and Notices to Airmen (NOTAMs) are collected and distributed. The agency has had its share of air traffic control SNAFUs, including one in 2023 that temporarily halted domestic flight departures nationwide after someone accidentally deleted a file from the NOTAM system. The FAA said it has already lined up five facilities to receive E-IDS upgrades: airports in Atlantic City, Nashville, and Rochester, New York, along with data processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City. The agency plans to install the system at 435 sites by the end of 2028. That 2028 deadline echoes the ambitious three-year timetable Duffy laid out last year for overhauling the nation's air traffic control system. Aside from the four systems E-IDS will replace, the FAA has a lot of outdated technology, with the Government Accountability Office saying in 2024 that 51 of the agency’s 138 ATC systems were unsustainable due to lack of parts and funding to sustain or replace them. Trump’s Big Beautiful Bill allocated $12.5 billion for the FAA’s overhaul efforts, but that’s far short of what’s actually needed. In December of last year, the FAA said that it needed an additional $20 billion to handle upgrade costs, and that appears to still be the case. "To continue modernizing our air traffic control facility, Secretary Duffy and FAA Administrator Bedford are calling on Congress to pass the Modern Skies Act," an FAA spokesperson told The Register in an email. The FAA said E-IDS will improve how Pilot Reports and Notices to Airmen (NOTAMs) are collected and distributed. The agency plans to install the system at 435 sites by the end of 2028. That 2028 deadline echoes the ambitious three-year timetable Duffy laid out last year for overhauling the nation's air traffic control system. Aside from the four systems E-IDS will replace, the FAA has a lot of outdated technology, with the Government Accountability Office saying in 2024 that 51 of the agency’s 138 ATC systems were unsustainable due to lack of parts and funding to sustain or replace them. Trump’s Big Beautiful Bill allocated $12.5 billion for the FAA’s overhaul efforts, but that’s far short of what’s actually needed. In December of last year, the FAA said that it needed an additional $20 billion to handle upgrade costs, and that appears to still be the case. "To continue modernizing our air traffic control facility, Secretary Duffy and FAA Administrator Bedford are calling on Congress to pass the Modern Skies Act," an FAA spokesperson told The Register in an email. That bill is asking for $30 billion to get ATC modernization across the finish line, the spokesperson added. " It will modernize our air traffic control system, replace crumbling aviation infrastructure, and build world-class airports across the country," they said. In other words, the FAA wants to get rid of floppy disks, but it's probably not accurate to say they're "out," as Duffy put it. The GAO said in September that the FAA was still well short of its financial needs, with an additional $10.2 billion needed for the second phase of upgrades, which has yet to receive a completion date. As with so many government ambitions, budgets often get in the way, and this wider modernization effort still seems more ambitious on paper than the FAA may be able to deliver. ®

item.title: You can see another galaxy with the naked eye — here's how to find it
item.description: null The first time I showed someone the Andromeda galaxy (M31), our conversation did not go quite as planned. I'd carefully worked my way across the sky, starting from the Great Square of Pegasus and hopping from star to star until I was confident I had the right patch. I pointed the telescope, got M31 in its crosshairs and proudly announced to my wife that I had found the closest giant galaxy to the Milky Way . Would she like to see it? She then stayed quiet for a little too long as she looked through the eyepiece. Then came an unexpected question. "Is it near that little smudge?" Hmmm. "Err, no. It is that little smudge," I replied. There was a pause. Of course, I knew exactly what had happened. We'd both seen photographs of M31 — a vast spiral galaxy with a brilliant center, sweeping dust lanes and hundreds of billions of stars. What we were actually looking at was a grayish blur that could easily have been mistaken for a mark on the eyepiece. That apparent disappointment is now my favorite part of finding Andromeda because the unimpressive smudge is real. The light entering your eyes has been traveling across space for about 2.5 million years. No screen, photograph or telescope is necessary. You are intercepting ancient light in your backyard. Technically, the Triangulum Galaxy (M33), about 2.7 million light-years away, can be seen with the naked eye, so it is therefore the most distant object the naked eye can see. But not mine — I've never seen it. M31 is a much more realistic naked-eye target. What's happening and when to look The Andromeda galaxy is at its most dramatic in photographs, not an eyepiece. (Image credit: Created using Canva and a base image from Starry Night) Early November is an excellent time to find M31 from the Northern Hemisphere. It's high and well placed during the evening, and this week the moon is becoming particularly cooperative. New Moon falls around Nov. 9, giving us several evenings with little or no moonlight to wash out faint deep-sky objects. I usually begin with the star Alpheratz, one of the corner stars of the Great Square of Pegasus. You go two stars left, two stars up, and you arrive at M31. Another route — and a good way to check you're in the right place — starts in Cassiopeia, the distinctive W-shaped constellation high in the northeastern sky on autumn evenings. You can use its second V-shape as an arrow pointing straight at M31. You can do that star-hop with the naked eye or a pair of binoculars, but M31 is visible to the naked eye only under a very dark sky. However, don't look for a miniature version of the photographs. Expect a faint, elongated patch with a slightly brighter middle. There's another beginner trap to avoid. Images make Andromeda look compact, but its full apparent extent is enormous — several times the width of the full moon — and our eyes usually pick up only the much brighter central region. Once you know that, the smudge starts making more sense. How and when I'm watching it Yo
item.dc:creator: Jamie Carter
item.content:encoded: null The first time I showed someone the Andromeda galaxy (M31), our conversation did not go quite as planned. I'd carefully worked my way across the sky, starting from the Great Square of Pegasus and hopping from star to star until I was confident I had the right patch. I pointed the telescope, got M31 in its crosshairs and proudly announced to my wife that I had found the closest giant galaxy to the Milky Way . Would she like to see it? She then stayed quiet for a little too long as she looked through the eyepiece. Then came an unexpected question. "Is it near that little smudge?" Hmmm. "Err, no. It is that little smudge," I replied. There was a pause. Of course, I knew exactly what had happened. We'd both seen photographs of M31 — a vast spiral galaxy with a brilliant center, sweeping dust lanes and hundreds of billions of stars. What we were actually looking at was a grayish blur that could easily have been mistaken for a mark on the eyepiece. That apparent disappointment is now my favorite part of finding Andromeda because the unimpressive smudge is real. The light entering your eyes has been traveling across space for about 2.5 million years. No screen, photograph or telescope is necessary. You are intercepting ancient light in your backyard. Technically, the Triangulum Galaxy (M33), about 2.7 million light-years away, can be seen with the naked eye, so it is therefore the most distant object the naked eye can see. But not mine — I've never seen it. M31 is a much more realistic naked-eye target. What's happening and when to look The Andromeda galaxy is at its most dramatic in photographs, not an eyepiece. (Image credit: Created using Canva and a base image from Starry Night) Early November is an excellent time to find M31 from the Northern Hemisphere. It's high and well placed during the evening, and this week the moon is becoming particularly cooperative. New Moon falls around Nov. 9, giving us several evenings with little or no moonlight to wash out faint deep-sky objects. I usually begin with the star Alpheratz, one of the corner stars of the Great Square of Pegasus. You go two stars left, two stars up, and you arrive at M31. Another route — and a good way to check you're in the right place — starts in Cassiopeia, the distinctive W-shaped constellation high in the northeastern sky on autumn evenings. You can use its second V-shape as an arrow pointing straight at M31. You can do that star-hop with the naked eye or a pair of binoculars, but M31 is visible to the naked eye only under a very dark sky. However, don't look for a miniature version of the photographs. Expect a faint, elongated patch with a slightly brighter middle. There's another beginner trap to avoid. Images make Andromeda look compact, but its full apparent extent is enormous — several times the width of the full moon — and our eyes usually pick up only the much brighter central region. Once you know that, the smudge starts making more sense. How and when I'm watching it You can use binoculars to find the Andromeda galaxy. (Image credit: Alan Dyer/Stocktrek Images via Getty Images) I'm going to look for Andromeda this week in the least heroic way possible. No expedition. No mountain-top observing location. No elaborate equipment. I'll wait until it is properly dark, step outside and then use Cassiopeia and the stars of Andromeda to work my way toward M31. I'll then reach for my 10x50 binoculars, which are rarely far from my side after dark, whether I'm at home or traveling. They gather enough light to make the galaxy's bright central region much more obvious without turning the exercise into a technical one. A really useful skill here — whether looking unaided or through binoculars — is averted vision. Instead of staring directly at the galaxy, look slightly beside it. The more light-sensitive parts of the retina away from the center of our vision can make faint objects easier to detect. It feels slightly ridiculous the first time you do it — deliberately not looking at the thing you're trying to see — but it works. If light pollution means you need binoculars, that still counts. No one gets a prize for detecting Andromeda unaided. After all, the extraordinary part isn't how you see it. It's what the light has done before reaching you. When those photons began their journey, modern humans did not exist. They crossed intergalactic space for roughly 2.5 million years and ended their trip in your retina. Stargazing is often described as looking back in time. With Andromeda, that phrase stops being a metaphor. Stargazer's corner: November 6-12, 2026 This wide-angle image shows the Cassiopeia, Perseus and Andromeda area of the northern autumn sky, including several deep-sky objects — including the Double Cluster, M31, M33, NGC 752 and M34. (Image credit: Alan Dyer/Stocktrek Images via Getty Images) This is the week you've been waiting for if you want to spend time on faint objects rather than fighting moonlight. Without a bright moon overhead, spend some time on Andromeda, but revisit the Double Cluster in Perseus (NGC 869 and NGC 884). Binoculars show it beautifully, and unlike M31, it becomes more obviously crowded with stars as you increase magnification. Two other large, bright open star clusters in this region that look great in 10x50 binoculars are the glittering stars of NGC 752 in Andromeda and M34, a bright, hazy patch in Perseus. Also keep an eye out for "shooting stars" because the Northern Taurid meteor shower peaks overnight on Nov. 11-12. Rates are low — around five meteors per hour under ideal conditions — so don't expect them to "light up the night sky". But they can produce bright, long-lasting 'fireballs' that can add a bit of pizzazz to a stargazing session. Constellation of the week: Andromeda Andromeda is well placed in the evening sky at this time of year. (Image credit: Created using Canva and a base image from Starry Night) Now that you've found its jewel, the Andromeda galaxy , it's worth trying to construct the constellation itself. As with M31, start with the Great Square of Pegasus and Alpheratz at its northeastern corner. Although it looks like part of the square, Alpheratz actually belongs to Andromeda. From Alpheratz, follow a curving line of stars away from the square through Mirach and on toward Almach. That gives you the basic shape of Andromeda — not the easiest constellation to imagine as a mythological princess, but a useful chain of stars to learn.

item.title: Mac lookalikes multiply as Linux raids Apple's wardrobe
item.description: Linux can do many things, but good looks aren't always its strong point. Apple has rather more of a reputation in that department, and a crop of new projects is bringing Mac-style polish to the open source desktop. Some are all-new, such as the Argentinian Lord OS , a whole new GUI desktop on top of Debian. Another, Cutefish , is a revival of a pre-ChatGPT project that never got as far as a complete release. Now it has version 1.0 for both x86-64 and Arm64, plus it's working on Mac binary compatibility via a work-in-progress layer called Reef . Ukrainian Desert OS is already at version 5.5 – practically a venerable elder in this company, despite appearing to be only about a year old. Meanwhile, ClokeOS uses Xfce for its desktop, but underneath, the OS is based on Apple's FOSS XNU kernel. The project lead plans to offer compatibility with multiple types of binaries: Linux apps, plus Mac apps via Darling , and Windows apps via Wine. This isn't new. Much as Cutefish has been revived, last year we reported on PearOS Linux , a very Mac-like skin on KDE Plasma. It has hooks in place for ambitious future features, such as Siri-style speech recognition. What's striking is the number of projects appearing and the pace of their development. Some offer both x86-64 and Arm64 builds, with Raspberry Pi editions in certain cases. For human coders, this would be months of hard work, but if it's just checking an additional box in an LLM development tool, then why wouldn't you? It's almost no extra work, but it widens the potential audience. Coveting Mac-like good looks is a longstanding urge among Linux users, and with legitimate reason. There's nothing wrong with Macs, even if you are mainly a FOSS user. We've written about the usefulness of FOSS apps on macOS before, including for reviving elderly Macs . Just a couple of months ago, we published a two-part guide on how to give Xfce a macOS-like layout and then how to tweak it so apps fit in better . We focused on the functionality, though, not the looks – we don't really care much for such things. If it does matter to you, though, you're not alone, and there are lots of themes and skins to make Xfce look prettier. item.dc:creator: Liam Proven
item.content:encoded: Linux can do many things, but good looks aren't always its strong point. Apple has rather more of a reputation in that department, and a crop of new projects is bringing Mac-style polish to the open source desktop. Some are all-new, such as the Argentinian Lord OS , a whole new GUI desktop on top of Debian. Another, Cutefish , is a revival of a pre-ChatGPT project that never got as far as a complete release. Now it has version 1.0 for both x86-64 and Arm64, plus it's working on Mac binary compatibility via a work-in-progress layer called Reef . Ukrainian Desert OS is already at version 5.5 – practically a venerable elder in this company, despite appearing to be only about a year old. Meanwhile, ClokeOS uses Xfce for its desktop, but underneath, the OS is based on Apple's FOSS XNU kernel. The project lead plans to offer compatibility with multiple types of binaries: Linux apps, plus Mac apps via Darling , and Windows apps via Wine. This isn't new. Much as Cutefish has been revived, last year we reported on PearOS Linux , a very Mac-like skin on KDE Plasma. It has hooks in place for ambitious future features, such as Siri-style speech recognition. What's striking is the number of projects appearing and the pace of their development. Some offer both x86-64 and Arm64 builds, with Raspberry Pi editions in certain cases. For human coders, this would be months of hard work, but if it's just checking an additional box in an LLM development tool, then why wouldn't you? It's almost no extra work, but it widens the potential audience. Coveting Mac-like good looks is a longstanding urge among Linux users, and with legitimate reason. There's nothing wrong with Macs, even if you are mainly a FOSS user. Modern macOS, or OS X as it was called a decade ago, is a Unix underneath its shiny proprietary desktop, and many of the flagship Linux FOSS apps also have Mac versions, from Firefox and Thunderbird, via LibreOffice, to VirtualBox, plus less well-known but very handy apps such as Ferdium and Panwriter. We've written about the usefulness of FOSS apps on macOS before, including for reviving elderly Macs . Just a couple of months ago, we published a two-part guide on how to give Xfce a macOS-like layout and then how to tweak it so apps fit in better . We focused on the functionality, though, not the looks – we don't really care much for such things. If it does matter to you, though, you're not alone, and there are lots of themes and skins to make Xfce look prettier. Some of these are all-in-one packages that you can install on an existing distro to give it a new look. One recent example is Cupertino , developed with assistance from Claude. From a few years ago, there are Small Sur and Ventura-Xfce . From nine years ago, long pre-LLM, there is osXFCE . We can see the appeal. From 2006 to 2020, Macs used Intel x86 processors, and those machines are now all falling off the end of Apple support – only four Intel models supported last year's macOS 26 "Tahoe," support for which is just starting to reach OpenCore Legacy Patcher. Earlier this year, The Reg FOSS desk upgraded his 11-year-old iMac to macOS 15 "Sequoia" with OCLP 2.5.1. The first experimental OCLP 3.0 release appeared last month, and it's now up to 3.0-rc5 . This adds support for macOS 26, Apple's final major macOS release for Intel Macs. That puts a ceiling on future macOS upgrades for both home-built Hackintoshes and older Macs kept going with unofficial patches. We gave LordOS a brief spin using its OVA virtual machine image. It installed and booted without trouble, and looks impressive. Last month, we wrote about ZacOS-9 and Mavernix , and similarly, we gave ZacOS-9 a very quick spin in a VM. The resemblance to our recent experience with ZacOS-9 went beyond appearances. In both, we found that the keyboard UI is largely missing: standard keystrokes didn't work. In LordOS, we found some menu options duplicated in two places in an un-Mac-like way, such as "About" options in both the app menu and the Help menu. The LordOS GitHub repository does not credit any LLM assistants, but it's gone though nine test releases in three weeks. The inevitable end of life of x86 Macs is driving fresh interest in FOSS OSes. They offer a life extension for genuine Macs as well as the enticing prospect of Mac-like polish for existing FOSS OSes. Combine that with the fast, easy code generation offered by LLM coding assistants, and we think there's going to be a lot more of this. In 2025, we saw one macOS-like Linux project rebooted. This October, we saw two new ones. In November, we've found four more. We have a feeling that these are just the first trickles of what may soon become a flood. ®

item.title: Oak Ridge labs gets hybrid quantum-HPC system to test qubit error correction
item.description: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) now boasts a system for research into quantum error correction, combining IBM quantum processors with a high-performance compute (HPC) system based on AMD silicon. The Quantum Science Center ( QSC ) at ORNL, funded by the US Department of Energy (DoE), unveiled what it calls a co-design platform for quantum error correction, marrying up quantum and HPC technology. While useful, fault-tolerant quantum systems always seem to be at least a decade away, there have been notable advances over the past several years in the field of quantum error correction, according to ORNL. These include early demonstrations of protecting quantum information from environmental noise, which can cause loss of the fragile quantum states needed for computations. "Solving the challenges of quantum error correction is essential to making quantum computing a practical tool for scientific discovery, which is a priority for Oak Ridge National Laboratory," said QSC director Travis Humble. IBM Fellow and director of IBM Research Jay Gambetta said that it was no longer a question of whether error correction works, but how to accelerate and optimize error correction to build systems that scientists can use to tackle challenging problems. "This new co-design platform for quantum error correction allows us to evaluate different approaches and determine the architectures, software and workflows that will scale," he stated. ORNL's new tool combines an IBM Quantum System Two, equipped with the latest 120-qubit Nighthawk r2 quantum processors , and Umbra, a classical HPC system powered by AMD 5th Gen Epyc CPUs and Instinct MI355X GPU accelerators. According to AMD, the CPUs provide the orchestration and general-purpose performance needed to coordinate everything, while the GPUs accelerate simulation, optimization and the parallel scientific computations surrounding quantum workloads. Also part of the system are AMD Versal SoCs to provide the low-latency control, readout and decoding capabilities for the quantum circuitry. ORNL says that this brings together the computing infrastructure needed for quantum error correction in a single environment, and opens it up to more researchers than ever before. They will use it to develop and validate quantum algorithms, workflows, and applications in an environment built for quantum-centric supercomputing, an emerging paradigm where quantum processors (QPUs), CPUs, and GPUs work together as one system. IBM says that one promising approach the co-design platform cloud explore is hierarchical error correction. It describes this as using an inner code to protect qubits within a module, while an outer code wraps around the inner code’s logical qubits and adds a second layer of protection. This approach could reach a trillion logical operations at a physical error rate of one in a thousand, IBM research suggested. The co-design platform is likely to play a key part in the DoE’s Quantum Genesis Mission objectives. These include the recently announced Q Competition , an initiative to deliver a system with 100 logical qubits capable of performing hundreds of millions of fault-tolerant operations. It follows an executive order from President Trump to develop a full-blown quantum system by 2028.®

item.title: Giant exoplanet emerges from the dark when the James Webb Space Telescope turns out the starlight
item.description: null Sometimes science can seem really counter-intuitive. For example, occasionally in astronomy, you can see more with less light. Case in point: the emergence of a giant planet in observations made by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), when astronomers found a way to block out light from the planet's parent star. The extrasolar planet, or exoplanet , in question is 51 Eridani b (51 ERI b), a gas giant with the same mass as around 11 Jupiters that orbits a star located around 97 light-years away. 51 ERI b was discovered back in 2015 by ground-based telescopes, but the planet was missing from observations of the system made by the JWST. That wasn't a failing of the JWST itself; no one is doubting the observing capabilities of the most powerful telescope humanity has ever hoisted into orbit around Earth. Instead, it was a result of starlight from the star 51 ERI A obscuring this intimidatingly massive world. The brightest planets are 100,000 times fainter than their host stars, meaning spotting them is like observing a firefly hovering around a lighthouse. Even using a tool called a coronagraph to block the star isn't enough to reveal the planet, as that doesn't stop all the starlight. The only solution to this glaring problem is a computer program to wipe out the starlight. "For the past 20 years, astronomers have tackled this problem by observing a different star and using its image as a reference," Jason Wang of Northwestern University explained in a statement . "Then, they subtract that reference image from the original observation to remove the unwanted glare to reveal faint planets that otherwise might be hidden." There is a problem with this process, however. Even the most stable telescopes "wobble." For instance, the JWST requires cryocoolers to keep its NIRCam instrument super cold, and those coolers have little motors that can cause the mirrors to vibrate. This movement, however slight, causes a scatter in starlight. The result is enough glare remaining to obscure a planet, but Wang and colleagues developed a new approach to this problem. Telescopes their more stable digital twins The new approach taken by the team is dubbed Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP), and it involves creating a digital "twin" of a telescope. Essentially a virtual replica that simulates how starlight travels through the telescope's mirrors and reaches its detectors. This twin is then fine-tuned to account for millions of tiny imperfections in the original telescope. The digital twin is then tweaked until it aligns with observations from the actual telescope. Astronomers can then remove the simulated glare from the original image. To assess the validity of the technique, the researchers took a second look at JWST observations of two star systems with known exoplanets, HIP 65426 and 51 Eridani , and one system, TYC 5899, with no known planets. The researchers found that, in terms of detecting faint exoplanets, FLIP outperformed conventional image

item.content:encoded: null Sometimes science can seem really counter-intuitive. For example, occasionally in astronomy, you can see more with less light. Case in point: the emergence of a giant planet in observations made by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), when astronomers found a way to block out light from the planet's parent star. That wasn't a failing of the JWST itself; no one is doubting the observing capabilities of the most powerful telescope humanity has ever hoisted into orbit around Earth. Instead, it was a result of starlight from the star 51 ERI A obscuring this intimidatingly massive world. The brightest planets are 100,000 times fainter than their host stars, meaning spotting them is like observing a firefly hovering around a lighthouse. Even using a tool called a coronagraph to block the star isn't enough to reveal the planet, as that doesn't stop all the starlight. The only solution to this glaring problem is a computer program to wipe out the starlight. "For the past 20 years, astronomers have tackled this problem by observing a different star and using its image as a reference," Jason Wang of Northwestern University explained in a statement . "Then, they subtract that reference image from the original observation to remove the unwanted glare to reveal faint planets that otherwise might be hidden." There is a problem with this process, however. Even the most stable telescopes "wobble." For instance, the JWST requires cryocoolers to keep its NIRCam instrument super cold, and those coolers have little motors that can cause the mirrors to vibrate. This movement, however slight, causes a scatter in starlight. The result is enough glare remaining to obscure a planet, but Wang and colleagues developed a new approach to this problem. Telescopes their more stable digital twins The new approach taken by the team is dubbed Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets (FLIP), and it involves creating a digital "twin" of a telescope. Essentially a virtual replica that simulates how starlight travels through the telescope's mirrors and reaches its detectors. This twin is then fine-tuned to account for millions of tiny imperfections in the original telescope. The digital twin is then tweaked until it aligns with observations from the actual telescope. Astronomers can then remove the simulated glare from the original image. To assess the validity of the technique, the researchers took a second look at JWST observations of two star systems with known exoplanets, HIP 65426 and 51 Eridani , and one system, TYC 5899, with no known planets. The researchers found that, in terms of detecting faint exoplanets, FLIP outperformed conventional image-processing techniques two to 15 times. This led to ERI b emerging from data collected by the JWST two years ago. "We showed that we can actually recover a planet that people previously couldn't see," Wang said. "This is real data in a real scenario. It was science left on the table because we didn’t have the right tools to analyze the data in the most optimal way." Left: JWST/NIRCam observation of star 51 Eridani A (51 Eri) in the F430M filter, using standard method KLIP to subtract the glare of the star. Middle: The same observation, but using new method FLIP to subtract the glare of the star. Right: Simulated image of 51 Eri b (Image credit: Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez.) The team hopes that FLIP can now be adopted by other astronomers in a bid to recover hitherto undiscovered exoplanets that have been hidden by the glare of their stars. This could be a major boon for NASA's proposed Habitable Worlds Observatory , which aims to directly photograph Earth-like planets orbiting distant sun-like stars. "We know of no planets around other stars that are like those in our own solar system," team leader Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez of Northwestern University said. "It's not that they don’t exist. It's that we cannot see them. "Every time we improve our techniques, we discover new types of planets. By finding more planets, we can better understand how planetary systems form and evolve, and ultimately how typical our own solar system truly is." The team's research was published on Wednesday (Nov. 4) in the journal Nature.

item.title: RIP to the world’s ugliest car
item.description: Elon Musk has hit the brakes on the Cybertruck, announcing on X that Tesla will wind down production at its Texas factory around mid-2027. Despite years of delays , the stainless-steel turd Musk claimed was a futuristic, apocalypse-proof tank straight out of Blade Runner is headed for a production wind-down after roughly four years, putting the Cybertruck alongside such automotive flops as the Edsel and the DeLorean. We can’t even put the Cybertruck on the same tier as the Ford Pinto, as that deathtrap was produced for a decade. The first Cybertruck lumbered off Tesla’s production line in mid-2023 before going on sale later that year , and it was practically right out of the gate that the problems began. Within months of the first deliveries, recall notices began piling up on the monstrosity. Trim pieces were flying off, internal components were failing, cameras were malfunctioning – all in all, the thing has faced 11 recalls since hitting the road in late 2023, most recently in April 2026, when a defect in brake rotors was found to potentially cause cracks that could allow wheel studs to separate from their hubs. Musk had pinned a lot of Tesla's hopes on the Cybertruck a few years ago, describing it during the company's Q3 2023 earnings call as "a great product" that would eventually generate "significant positive cash flow" for Tesla. Musk said on that same earnings call that Tesla intended to ramp Cybertruck production up to 250,000 vehicles per year by 2025 to meet the over one million Cybertruck reservations he claimed Tesla had taken. Some Musk fans may still be waiting for their Cybertrucks, while others may have canceled their reservations after reading early reviews or experiencing the reality of driving such an ugly vehicle associated with a right-wing provocateur. Tesla hasn't disclosed how many reservations were canceled or converted into sales. Even then, it was widely reported in recent years that unsold Cybertrucks were piling up around the US, with Tesla unable to move them even with repeated price reductions. Tesla has never shared Cybertruck sales numbers, but it’s estimated that only around 70,000 of the things have been sold in the past three years - not exactly a ringing endorsement of its marketability. So that’s that for the Cybertruck - it’s safe to say it’s been a total disaster for Musk and Tesla. It never sold well, never became a boat , and will likely never be remembered fondly. ®

item.title: DoJ's 'Super Intelligence Task Force' up and running
item.description: The US Department of Justice (DoJ) says its Super Intelligence Task Force (SINTF) is now up and running, after president Donald Trump ordered the move in a memo last month. Headed up by director of national intelligence Jay Clayton, as well as associate attorney general Stanley Woodward and associate deputy attorney general Stephen Weiss, SINTF's responsibility is to protect the US's lead in artificial intelligence development. Thursday's announcement, which was littered with the " super intelligence " Trumpism, said the task force will ensure the US's SI/AI leadership remains uncompromised by foreign AI "abuse," including by state and state-backed groups, criminal enterprises, individuals, or corporate entities. Per Trump's October 13 memo [PDF], SITF will take "affirmative measures, as appropriate," to ensure the US stays ahead in AI development. It did not elaborate on what this nebulous phrase meant, but it can be reasonably assumed this means a breadth of proactive steps. The memo also stated that the task force will organize the DoJ's criminal and civil lawsuits involving AI, recommend enforcement priorities concerning public safety and AI misuse, develop prosecution guidance for unlawful AI conduct, and feed into legislative proposals to prevent "burdensome regulation." Addressing a Wall Street Journal tech conference this week, Pentagon CTO and SITF vice chair Emil Michael said the team would release details about its AI regulatory landscape later this month. The task force will also shoulder various cross-departmental responsibilities, such as "deconflicting investigations, cases, and other matters" among departments and the offices of US attorneys. According to quotes from senior officials, chief among the concerns facing ordinary US citizens are AI attacks that target individuals, as well as those that aim to disrupt critical infrastructure and other national security interests. "The creation of the DOJ-SITF marks an important moment for the Department to help advance SI technologies and, at the same time, protect American innovation," said Weiss. "The Department also has a responsibility to utilize law enforcement tools at our disposal to deter improper use of SI, harden regular reporting on SI risk and response, and ensure companies exercise vigorous internal controls so that SI technology behaves as intended. The Department is committed to protecting all Americans and our business interests." Trump compelled the US to start using the term "super intelligence" in September, claiming "artificial intelligence," the widely used and original term coined in the mid-1950s, was a better descriptor for the technology's capabilities. The US government's dedicated website for SI states that "America is in a race for Super Intelligence. We intend to win it." It also highlights a number of initiatives the government has taken to promote its AI supremacy, including legal guidance to streamline federal approvals, leading to more data centers being

The Department is committed to protecting all Americans and our business interests." Trump compelled the US to start using the term "super intelligence" in September, claiming "artificial intelligence," the widely used and original term coined in the mid-1950s, was a better descriptor for the technology's capabilities. The US government's dedicated website for SI states that "America is in a race for Super Intelligence. We intend to win it." It also highlights a number of initiatives the government has taken to promote its AI supremacy, including legal guidance to streamline federal approvals, leading to more data centers being built. The pivot toward renaming the technology in all official capacities raised confusion at the time. A somewhat contradictory move, the Trump administration heavily promotes its own AI innovators, but in one swoop essentially antiquated the trading name of arguably its most recognizable AI lab, OpenAI. One financier previously floated the idea that Trump ordered the shift to boost the value of .si domain names , many of which have recently been registered using MAGA-related terms and resold for millions of dollars. There is no categorical evidence that the investments are linked to the Trump family, however. ®

item.title: Hera probe gets 1st good look at asteroid system clobbered by NASA's DART mission | Space photo of the day for Nov. 6, 2026
item.description: null The Didymos binary asteroid system, as seen by Europe's Hera probe. The main asteroid, Didymos, dominates the frame while just a sliver of its "moonlet," Dimorphos, is visible beneath it. ESA released this image on Nov. 5, 2026. (Image credit: ESA) The European Space Agency 's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has gotten its first close-up look at the Didymos binary asteroid system. If that system sounds familiar, it's because it made headlines in September 2022 when NASA's DART (Double Asteroid Redirection Test) spacecraft smashed into it. The aim of the DART mission was to test whether an impact could divert an asteroid away from a collision course with Earth. The purpose of Hera is to follow up on DART by making up-close observations of the Didymos system. "The first thing we said was, 'Wow,'" Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel said in a statement about the image, which ESA released on Thursday (Nov. 5). "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART’s camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world." What is it? The Didymos system consists of the eponymous 2,560-foot-wide (780 meters) space rock and its "moonlet" Dimorphos, which is about 530 feet (160 m) in diameter. The DART mission impacted Dimorphos on Sept. 26, 2022, with the aim of causing a change in the orbital period of the moonlet. And it worked: Before the impact, Dimorphos completed one lap around Didymos in around 11 hours and 55 minutes. The DART collision reduced the length of this period by around 33 minutes. The change is a result of the fact that Dimporphos is now traveling at around 2.7 millimeters per second more slowly than it did before the collision. The newly released photo shows Didymos in detail. Just a sliver of Dimorphos is visible, below and slightly to the left of the main asteroid. Why is it incredible? The changes caused by DART were small. But in a real Earth-threatening scenario, even such a tiny shift could help divert an asteroid on a collision course — as long as scientists get enough advance warning of its approach. Hera's observations should help reveal what other changes have occurred on and around Didymos. Scientists are already seeing that, while Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator as before the impact, many changes have occurred. This includes the creation of multiple boulders, craters, and patterns of grooves or ridges. "Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 kilometer [0.62 miles] of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out," said Michael Kueppers, ESA’s Hera mission scientist. "We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify." Stay tuned to Space.com for more Hera findings from Didymos.

item.title: FinTribe Finance Fair 2026: Empowers Over 10,000 Women to Build Wealth and Financial Independence
item.description: Over 10,000 women gathered at the Landmark Event Centre, Victoria Island, Lagos, on October 31, 2026, for the fourth edition of FinTribe Finance Fair , a growing movement dedicated to helping African women move from financial awareness to wealth creation and ownership. Themed I CAN and powered by returning lead sponsor Sycamore, the event brought together financial experts, business leaders, entrepreneurs and influential personalities, including Funke Akindele , Omoni Oboli , BamBam , Sola Adesakin and Olufemi Shobanjo , for a day of practical financial education, inspiring conversations and meaningful opportunities. For FinTribe founder Jennifer Awirigwe , popularly known as Financial Jennifer, the fair represents a bigger mission: helping women gain the confidence and resources to take charge of their financial futures. “Financial education is important, but knowledge must eventually become action. We want women to leave Finance Fair knowing that they can save, invest, grow their income, build businesses and take ownership of their financial future,” she shared ahead of the event. Beyond Finance Fair, FinTribe is building a community where women learn about money and put that knowledge into practice . With a presence across 43 countries, the organisation has reached over 20,000 women through financial education, supported more than 5,000 women with capital market training and helped members collectively save and invest millions of dollars. Through its Wealth Builders Academy, savings and investment community, real estate initiatives and recently launched FinTribe App, the organisation continues to create opportunities for women to build healthier financial habits, develop investment confidence and work towards long-term financial independence. At the fair, award-winning filmmaker Omoni Oboli encouraged women to pursue their ambitions without neglecting their wellbeing, reminding them to take things one step at a time, prioritise rest and ask for help when needed. During the Financial Clinic, Sola Adesakin challenged women to become more intentional about their finances, emphasising the importance of earning, budgeting and turning income into real assets. She also introduced the four forces of money: Earnings, Expenses, Engines and Encumbrances. Olufemi Shobanjo of NGX Regulation Limited shared insights into capital market participation, while actress BamBam, marketing strategist and Woof Studios founder Adetutu Laditan, and Mercy Agbeti, popularly known as Christian Money Woman, contributed to conversations about building value, navigating opportunities and growing with purpose. The entrepreneur later shared on her instagram page that “she had saved to purchase a VIP ticket to the fair and had admired Funke for years”. The fair also featured empowerment opportunities and giveaways, including children’s investment portfolios, stock units, a plot of land, a Zanzibar trip and getaway experiences supported by partner organisations. Sycamore returned as lead sponsor for the second consecutive year, alongside other partners supporting FinTribe’s mission to expand women’s access to financial knowledge and opportunities. From its first edition in 2023 to this year’s gathering, FinTribe Finance Fair has continued to demonstrate the power of bringing women together around a shared goal. But the real work continues long after the event ends. item.title: Crowd fave Linux Mint update approaches, fresh from autumn release of Cinnamon desktop
item.description: Linux Mint 27 is expected next month, and it's starting to take shape. Its flagship desktop, Cinnamon 2.8, is already available. The team behind the popular, beginner-friendly Linux just released Cinnamon 2.8 , which will be the default desktop in Mint 27. Since 2014, Linux Mint versions have been based on the LTS releases of Ubuntu. Since a new LTS, Ubuntu 26.04 "Resolute Raccoon" arrived in late April , that means that a corresponding version of Mint is in development. The Mint project blog post last month revealed the codename: "Adrien." This is the first male codename since Mint 1.0 "Ada" in 2006, based on the first ever Ubuntu LTS release, 6.06 "Dapper Drake", but the project has run through the whole alphabet since then (except for the letter “Y”.) That blog also revealed it will have a new alarm clock app, but the subsequent Mint Blog post imparted more information. The Nemo file manager will gain a preview pane, there will be a new and much more capable system resource-monitor program called "Superlight", a new simple manager for compressed archive files (Zip and so on) called "Unfold," and a new, theme-able terminal emulator called "Velocitty." Mint also has a new Community Website , which uses GitHub to manage logins and eliminates the old website's dependency on PHP. Probably the most significant new feature, though, is that Mint 27 will restore system hibernation. Ubuntu supported hibernation in its early releases, but it has been disabled as standard since 12.04 "Precise Pangolin." Enabling it again is regularly discussed, for instance back in 2020 . As we discussed in some detail a year ago , it's a complicated subject and there's a lot that can go wrong. It seems that Mint's Clément Lefebvre feels he can sort this, and we hope it works out. Support is included in the new version of Cinnamon, among a host of other changes. Its Wayland support is no longer experimental, although the X11 session is still there so users won't be forced to use the new system. The Network Manager applet has better, simpler VPN support and Wi-Fi encryption handling. There are multiple improvements across the desktop: better handling of sound devices, keyboard input layouts, touchpads and gesture support, HiDPI display handling, and better search in the Settings app. The window list control has been upgraded, more things happen in the background for faster desktop starts, and it has better handling and storage of authentication and credentials, including the same Rust-based "oo7" secret store we mentioned in Fedora 45 . Screensaver handling is also mentioned – this is particularly problematic under Wayland, as XScreensaver maintainer Jamie Zawinski has covered with some feeling . The Mint blog mentioned this at the start of 2026 , when Lefebvre announced the new, slower, annual release schedule. item.content:encoded: Linux Mint 27 is expected next month, and it's starting to take shape. Its flagship desktop, Cinnamon 2.8, is already available. The team behind the popular, beginner-friendly Linux just released Cinnamon 2.8 , which will be the default desktop in Mint 27. Since a new LTS, Ubuntu 26.04 "Resolute Raccoon" arrived in late April , that means that a corresponding version of Mint is in development. This is the first male codename since Mint 1.0 "Ada" in 2006, based on the first ever Ubuntu LTS release, 6.06 "Dapper Drake", but the project has run through the whole alphabet since then (except for the letter “Y”.) That blog also revealed it will have a new alarm clock app, but the subsequent Mint Blog post imparted more information. The Nemo file manager will gain a preview pane, there will be a new and much more capable system resource-monitor program called "Superlight", a new simple manager for compressed archive files (Zip and so on) called "Unfold," and a new, theme-able terminal emulator called "Velocitty." Mint also has a new Community Website , which uses GitHub to manage logins and eliminates the old website's dependency on PHP. Probably the most significant new feature, though, is that Mint 27 will restore system hibernation. Ubuntu supported hibernation in its early releases, but it has been disabled as standard since 12.04 "Precise Pangolin." Enabling it again is regularly discussed, for instance back in 2020 . As we discussed in some detail a year ago , it's a complicated subject and there's a lot that can go wrong. It seems that Mint's Clément Lefebvre feels he can sort this, and we hope it works out. Support is included in the new version of Cinnamon, among a host of other changes. Its Wayland support is no longer experimental, although the X11 session is still there so users won't be forced to use the new system. The Network Manager applet has better, simpler VPN support and Wi-Fi encryption handling. There are multiple improvements across the desktop: better handling of sound devices, keyboard input layouts, touchpads and gesture support, HiDPI display handling, and better search in the Settings app. The window list control has been upgraded, more things happen in the background for faster desktop starts, and it has better handling and storage of authentication and credentials, including the same Rust-based "oo7" secret store we mentioned in Fedora 45 . Screensaver handling is also mentioned – this is particularly problematic under Wayland, as XScreensaver maintainer Jamie Zawinski has covered with some feeling . The Mint blog mentioned this at the start of 2026 , when Lefebvre announced the new, slower, annual release schedule. LXQt 2.5 Cinnamon is not the only desktop environment that has moved to embrace Wayland while also maintaining its support for X.org. Almost exactly two years ago, we reported that the LXQt 2.1 included preliminary Wayland support . That project is very much still in active development, led by Jen-Lee "PCMan" Hong, and version 2.5.0 just appeared, almost simultaneously with Cinnamon 2.8. Before LXQt, "PCMan" developed the LXDE desktop – which is still around. There's an LXDE spin of Fedora 45, the Raspberry Pi OS uses some of its components, and last year when Debian 13 was released we also noted that its terminal emulator, LXTerminal, had just been updated. This release of LXQt removes its last dependency on an LXDE component – until now, it still used the old menu-cache . LXQt 2.5 is based on Qt 6.10, and it draws upon some of the components of KDE Plasma. One of these is libkscreen , which manages screens for Plasma. Version 6.8 of this drops X11 support – as does Plasma 6.8 itself – and that broke LXQt's Monitor Settings applet. The team are looking for a workaround and plan to fix this in a minor point release. Aside from this, the desktop's taskbar-style panel has improved sizing support, icon handling, and auto-hide, but most of the improvements in this release are in around its QTerminal terminal emulator. New LXQt versions usually appear twice a year, around April and November, so this version will likely be in Lubuntu 27.04 in about five months – and available in many other distributions, too. ®

item.title: Blue Origin unveils more thrust, less haste as New Glenn slips to 2027
item.description: New Glenn's return to flight has slipped to January 2027, according to the internal memo, viewed by The Register, from Blue Origin CEO Dave Limp, overshadowing the company's announcements of a new third stage and booster engine. Blue Origin has been rebuilding after its New Glenn rocket exploded during a ground test in May , extensively damaging the launchpad. A month later, the company's CEO, Dave Limp, said that Blue Origin "still plan[s] to fly again this year," which raised a few eyebrows in the space and rocket community. The detonation had pretty much destroyed the facility, and getting back into the launch business so quickly seemed optimistic. That timetable has now slipped. In the memo, Limp praised the team's efforts but said: "We're proactively updating our anticipated launch date to January 2027." A small slip given the damage, but one that leaves less breathing room before NASA's planned Artemis III demonstration mission, involving lunar technologies from Blue Origin and SpaceX, next year. The delay emerged as the Bezos-backed company unveiled GS3, a third stage for New Glenn , designed for missions including direct injection into geostationary orbit and Earth-escape trajectories. The company said: "GS3 is already under contract for a cislunar mission with a government customer scheduled to launch in 2028." Blue Origin says the stage is not required for its lunar lander architecture, although it could support sustained operations around the Moon. The company also unveiled Northstar , a booster engine it says has half the parts and 30 percent less mass than its BE-4, while increasing thrust from 640,000 to 715,000 pounds-force. The memo said the team had "found and fixed the issue that caused the anomaly," without elaborating. Limp said in August that the problem "originated at the main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines" and that existing engines would need retrofitting, but did not explain how the valve failed or what changes were required. The memo added that the company would "continue sharing progress updates on Voyager ." ®

item.title: Northern lights could reach New York and Idaho this weekend as speedy solar wind races toward Earth
item.description: null The northern lights could put on an impressive display this weekend as a colossal coronal hole on the sun fires a stream of high-speed solar wind toward Earth. Minor (G1) geomagnetic storm conditions between Nov. 6 and Nov. 8, with a chance of moderate (G2) conditions on Nov. 7 and Nov. 8, according to NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) . If G2 conditions materialize, the northern lights could be visible as far south as New York and Idaho. What is happening? The culprit behind the potential uptick in northern lights is a large coronal hole on the sun , a region where the sun's magnetic field opens up. They allow streams of charged particles known as the solar wind to escape more easily into space. Coronal holes appear darker in ultraviolet images because they are cooler and less dense than their surroundings. And this particularly large — and rather oddly shaped — coronal hole is sending some seriously speedy wind our way. The culprit is a large coronal hole in the sun, shaped a bit like a witch on a broom... (Image credit: NASA SDO) The U.K. Met Office forecasts solar wind speeds between 342 and 404 miles (550-650 kilometers) per second, considerably faster than the typical speed of around 249 miles (400 km) per second. The fast solar winds are expected to arrive around Nov. 6-7 and could persist through much of the weekend. It could interact with Earth's magnetic field , potentially triggering geomagnetic storms and fueling spectacular aurora shows. The stronger the storm, the farther south the northern lights can potentially be seen. A predictive model from NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center showing speedy solar wind (radial velocity image lower left) arriving at Earth (green dot) around Nov. 6 and persisting through Nov. 9. (Image credit: NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center) Where will auroras be visible? Under G1 conditions, auroras may be visible from northern Michigan and Maine, but if activity intensifies to G2 levels, skywatchers farther south, including those in New York and Idaho, could be in for a treat. But remember! Aurora forecasts are notoriously tricky. Much depends on the strength and orientation of the magnetic field carried by the incoming solar wind, particularly whether it points southward, allowing more energy to transfer to Earth's magnetic field. Northern Hemisphere aurora forecast courtesy of the U.K. Met Office To give yourself the best chance of seeing the northern lights, keep an eye on those aurora forecasts, head somewhere dark away from city lights if you can, with a view of the northern horizon. To stay updated on space weather and know the best times and places to catch auroras, consider using a space weather app tailored to your location. One app I recommend is "My Aurora Forecast & Alerts," available on both iOS and Android . Another great tool is the "Space Weather Live" app on iOS and Android , which offers more in-depth insights into current space weather conditions and their potential

item.content:encoded: null The northern lights could put on an impressive display this weekend as a colossal coronal hole on the sun fires a stream of high-speed solar wind toward Earth. Minor (G1) geomagnetic storm conditions between Nov. 6 and Nov. 8, with a chance of moderate (G2) conditions on Nov. 7 and Nov. 8, according to NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC) . If G2 conditions materialize, the northern lights could be visible as far south as New York and Idaho. What is happening? The culprit behind the potential uptick in northern lights is a large coronal hole on the sun , a region where the sun's magnetic field opens up. They allow streams of charged particles known as the solar wind to escape more easily into space. Coronal holes appear darker in ultraviolet images because they are cooler and less dense than their surroundings. And this particularly large — and rather oddly shaped — coronal hole is sending some seriously speedy wind our way. The culprit is a large coronal hole in the sun, shaped a bit like a witch on a broom... (Image credit: NASA SDO) The U.K. Met Office forecasts solar wind speeds between 342 and 404 miles (550-650 kilometers) per second, considerably faster than the typical speed of around 249 miles (400 km) per second. The fast solar winds are expected to arrive around Nov. 6-7 and could persist through much of the weekend. It could interact with Earth's magnetic field , potentially triggering geomagnetic storms and fueling spectacular aurora shows. The stronger the storm, the farther south the northern lights can potentially be seen. A predictive model from NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center showing speedy solar wind (radial velocity image lower left) arriving at Earth (green dot) around Nov. 6 and persisting through Nov. 9. (Image credit: NOAA's Space Weather Prediction Center) Where will auroras be visible? Under G1 conditions, auroras may be visible from northern Michigan and Maine, but if activity intensifies to G2 levels, skywatchers farther south, including those in New York and Idaho, could be in for a treat. But remember! Aurora forecasts are notoriously tricky. Much depends on the strength and orientation of the magnetic field carried by the incoming solar wind, particularly whether it points southward, allowing more energy to transfer to Earth's magnetic field. Northern Hemisphere aurora forecast courtesy of the U.K. Met Office To give yourself the best chance of seeing the northern lights, keep an eye on those aurora forecasts, head somewhere dark away from city lights if you can, with a view of the northern horizon. To stay updated on space weather and know the best times and places to catch auroras, consider using a space weather app tailored to your location. One app I recommend is "My Aurora Forecast & Alerts," available on both iOS and Android . Another great tool is the "Space Weather Live" app on iOS and Android , which offers more in-depth insights into current space weather conditions and their potential for aurora activity.

item.title: DigiCert admits 16-month security lapse exposed customer information
item.description: DigiCert has admitted that a botched server migration left an internal system exposed to the internet for more than a year, allowing an unauthorized user to access customer data, including passports, driver's licenses, and other identity documents. The certificate authority has begun notifying affected customers but has yet to disclose how many people had their information exposed. In an email seen by The Register , DigiCert confirmed the compromised information included names, business email addresses, phone numbers, and business addresses. Some records may also have contained passports, driver's licenses, utility bills, or other identification documents. "We are completing a review of identification documents to determine the specific individuals involved," DigiCert told those affected, adding that it would notify those people once the review was complete. DigiCert's incident report traces the blunder back to February 2025, when an internal business system was moved from a VPN-protected network to a different availability zone. That change also opened the system up to the public internet, where it sat for more than 16 months without DigiCert realizing. The archive used the same account management platform as DigiCert's customer-facing products, including a self-registration feature that was never supposed to be available on the internal system. This allowed outsiders to create accounts without multifactor authentication and, thanks to a separate permissions flaw, use them to browse archived customer records. DigiCert found the unauthorized accounts on June 18, 2026, but initially dismissed them as harmless because they weren't assigned to an application. A security researcher raised the alarm about the account creation issue three days later, but it took until July 2 for DigiCert to shut it down. Unfortunately, someone had already been poking around. It wasn't until October 12 that DigiCert began investigating whether customer information had actually been accessed. On October 19, it confirmed that an unauthorized account had accessed a subset of archived records between June 27 and July 2. DigiCert described the affected records as a "small proportion" of its archive but hasn't disclosed how many customers or individuals were caught up in the breach. The company did not respond to The Register ’s questions at the time of publication. DigiCert's postmortem makes for uncomfortable reading. The server move didn't get a proper security review, monitoring failed to pick up suspicious activity, and the access controls weren't much use against self-registered accounts. The company has since switched off self-registration, tightened network access, and added monitoring that might have come in handy a few months earlier. Certificate authority operations, CertCentral, and DigiCert ONE were unaffected, the company said, adding that customer credentials and issued certificates remain secure. DigiCert found the unauthorized accounts on June 18, 2026, but initially dismissed them as harmless because they weren't assigned to an application. A security researcher raised the alarm about the account creation issue three days later, but it took until July 2 for DigiCert to shut it down. Unfortunately, someone had already been poking around. It wasn't until October 12 that DigiCert began investigating whether customer information had actually been accessed. The company has since switched off self-registration, tightened network access, and added monitoring that might have come in handy a few months earlier. Certificate authority operations, CertCentral, and DigiCert ONE were unaffected, the company said, adding that customer credentials and issued certificates remain secure. It also found no evidence that the unauthorized account had been used to issue, revoke, or validate certificates. That’s good news for anyone worried about their certificates, but less so for those who handed DigiCert a copy of their passport. ®

item.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has revived the midnight game launch – but was it worth the wait?
item.description: When our writer found himself among the hundreds on Oxford Street hoping to get their hands on early copies and collectibles, it was a heartwarming reminder of the shared experience of fandom • The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true It is Thursday night and I am sat blurry-eyed and runny nosed outside the Argos on Oxford Street. Incredibly, I am far from alone. This is not some strange protest against the popular retailer. When the clock strikes midnight, the lavish 4K Switch 2 remake of beloved N64 classic The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will be released, and I have joined a lengthy queue of about 500 fans desperate to snag early copies. There are similar events taking place across the world, from Melbourne to Mexico City; at key locations, Nintendo has senior executives waiting at the tills. These days, of course, most video games are bought as digital copies that download straight to your PC or console on the day of release. You don’t even have to get out of bed to start playing. But in a bygone era, when we used to go to shops to buy games, midnight launches offered a space for likeminded enthusiasts to gather and celebrate their fandom. Every Call of Duty, Halo or Grand Theft Auto release would have fans queueing outside branches of Game or Electronics Boutique, many dressed as favourite characters. Continue reading...

item.title: Max Power: NASA hosting its 1st air show this weekend on Florida's Space Coast
item.description: null NASA will host a first-of-its-kind air show and aerospace expo on Florida's Space Coast this weekend. The show, called Max Power, will take place Saturday and Sunday (Nov. 7 and Nov. 8) at and around NASA's Kennedy Space Center (KSC). That name should be familiar to "Simpsons" fans, by the way: Max Power is an alias that Homer uses in the 13th episode of the show's 10th season. (He got it off a hair dryer.) There will be a lot to see at NASA's event, so you should consider dropping by if you're on the Space Coast this weekend. (Tickets are required; you can buy them here .) Here are a few of the highlights. Saturday, Nov. 7 (all times local, EST): 11:15-11:30 a.m.: Overview of NASA's "quiet" supersonic jet, the X-59 12:30-1:00 p.m.: Discussion of NASA's science and exploration goals by Nicky Fox and Lori Glaze (the heads of NASA's Science Mission Directorate and Human Spaceflight Mission Directorate, respectively) 12:45-1:00 p.m.: Q&A with the four astronauts of NASA's Artemis III mission 1:00-1:30 p.m.: "How Is NASA Preparing Astronauts to Live and Work on the Moon?" with Suzanne Bell, who leads NASA’s Behavioral Health and Performance Laboratory at Johnson Space Center 1:30-2:00 p.m.: Discussion of NASA's planned lunar outpost , with Moon Base program head Carlos García-Galán 2:00-2:30 p.m.: Summary of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope mission, by senior project scientist Julie McEnery Sunday, Nov. 8 11:15-11:30 a.m.: "How NASA uses aircraft for research! Topic: Connecting flight to research" 12:45-1:15 p.m.: Update on the U.S. Space Academy with NASA Deputy Administrator Matt Anderson 12:45-1:00 p.m. (different stage): Q&A with NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, of SpaceX's Crew-12 mission to the International Space Station 1:00-1:30 p.m.: Discussion of SR-1 Freedom, NASA's planned nuclear-powered spacecraft that will launch mini-helicopters to Mars in 2028 1:30-2:00 p.m.: "The X-Factor: NASA's Flight Revolution Topic: X-Planes" 2:00-2:30 p.m.: Conversation with an (as yet unnamed) NASA astronaut 3:00-3:15: "In the Cockpit: Meet the NASA Pilots!" NASA's Freedom 250 F-5 team, including NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, performs a flyover during the national anthem at an NFL game between the Cleveland Browns and the Carolina Panthers in Cleveland on Sept. 27, 2026. It will feature Fox, García-Galán, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and Dayna Ise, the acting director of the Utility and Infrastructure Office for the Moon Base Program. (He funded and commanded SpaceX's Inspiration4 and Polaris Dawn missions, which flew to Earth orbit in September 2021 and September 2024, respectively.) The event "will showcase the newest aircraft, autonomous vehicles, technologies, and more defining the future of air and space," agency officials wrote in a Max Power description . "NASA will display its quiet supersonic X-59 plane, and agency partners will showcase moon rovers, spacecraft and more."

item.title: Home Office cloud services contract may net AWS £1B
item.description: Amazon Web Services (AWS) looks set to win more than a billion pounds of UK taxpayers' money under a new Home Office contract for public cloud hosting. A planning notice , published on October 30, covers the renewal of the department's public cloud services, to meet its current and future hosting needs. The estimated value is £881,621,007 ($1.18 billion), which passes £1 billion once VAT is included. AWS won the existing contract with the Home Office in 2023 for about £450 million (c $603 million). The Register has asked the Home Office why the figure has risen so much, and will update this article if it responds. Once awarded, the contract is expected to run from December 2027 to December 2029, with a possible extension to December 2031 (four years in total). A market engagement event for suppliers on the G-Cloud 15 Lot 1A procurement framework is scheduled for December 8, giving bidders the chance to pitch. The Home Office would not say who else is being considered, saying it does not comment on ongoing procurement. The notice lands as digital sovereignty becomes a bigger problem in the UK and across Europe, amid suspicion that US authorities have cut off access to American technology for political reasons . A survey found that about three-quarters of businesses in the UK, France, and Germany fear Washington could abruptly sever access to the US tech platforms they rely on. Earlier this year, the Open Rights Group warned politicians that the UK is far too dependent on US technology companies to run critical operations. Whitehall is mindful of its over-reliance on American hyperscalers. As The Register revealed in 2024, the Cabinet Office admitted - in an internal document seen by us - that the government’s negotiating power had been inhibited by vendor lock-in . It said the "UK government’s current approach to cloud adoption and management across its departments faces several challenges" which combined result "in risk concentration and vendor lock-in that inhibit UK government’s negotiating power over the cloud vendors." It acknowledged "the existing dominance of AWS and Azure in the UK Government’s cloud services is set to continue." A source at one supplier that works with the public sector said the UK administration was "failing to support UK [cloud] providers, it says they can’t meet scale and that is garbage." They claimed that in many cases the government people writing the tenders are advised by professional services companies to favor the hyperscalers. The professional services companies are then "rewarded" as migration or integration partners, our source claimed. The UK government also pledged to steer more business to small-to-medium sized enterprises (SMEs) in an action plan published last month. In August it added smaller, local suppliers to G-Cloud 15 , though a place on the framework does not guarantee any business. The UK government also pledged to steer more business to small-to-medium sized enterprises (SMEs) in an action plan published last month.
